posts.format: What an economic change means for students

slides.title: What inflation does to your money
slides.sub: Prices rose 3.7% in a year. Gas rose 34.2%. Here's what that means for you.

slides.heading: What CPI measures
body: The Consumer Price Index (CPI) tracks what a set basket of everyday things costs: food, rent, gas, phone plans, haircuts. Inflation is how fast that basket gets more expensive.
From September 2025 to September 2026, the basket rose 3.7%. Leave out food and energy (called core inflation) and it rose 2.6%.

slides.heading: Why gas hurts most
body: Energy prices rose 20.4% in a year, and gasoline alone rose 34.2%. That's why overall inflation (3.7%) is well above core inflation (2.6%).
Example: a tank that cost $40 a year ago now costs about $53.68. Fill up once a week and that's about $711 more a year.

slides.heading: Your raise vs. inflation
body: Get a 3% raise while prices rise 3.7% and you can buy a little less than last year. Economists call that a drop in your real wage.
Savings work the same way. Money earning less than the inflation rate loses buying power, so compare your savings rate to inflation.

slides.takeaway: If your money grows slower than prices, you're losing buying power.

posts.caption:
New inflation numbers come out today at 8:30 AM ET. Here's how to read them.

The latest reading (September 2026) shows prices up 3.7% in a year. Core inflation, which leaves out food and energy, was 2.6%. The gap comes from energy: gasoline rose 34.2% in a year. A tank that cost $40 a year ago costs about $53.68 now (example).

The money lesson: if your pay or your savings grow slower than prices, you can buy less than before. A 3% raise with 3.7% inflation is a small pay cut in real terms.

Data: U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics, CPI for September 2026 (released Oct. 14, 2026).

Follow @hflic.hebron for a new money lesson every day.

Education only, not financial advice.
